title: 04 — Storage Formats and Layout
html:
04 — Storage Formats and Layout

The one idea: analytical performance is mostly decided before any query runs — by the file format (columnar or not), the table format on top of it (transactions and statistics), and the physical layout (how rows are grouped into files). The fastest query is the one that can prove it does not need to read most of the data.

1. Row vs columnar storage

Consider a table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, amount, notes) with 1 billion rows.

---
title: Row vs columnar layout of the same three rows
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph ROW["Row-oriented file"]
        R1["1, C7, 2026-09-01, PAID, 40.00, ..."]
        R2["2, C9, 2026-09-01, NEW, 12.50, ..."]
        R3["3, C7, 2026-09-02, PAID, 99.90, ..."]
    end
    subgraph COL["Column-oriented file"]
        C1["order_id: 1, 2, 3"]
        C2["customer_id: C7, C9, C7"]
        C3["order_date: 2026-09-01, 2026-09-01, 2026-09-02"]
        C4["status: PAID, NEW, PAID"]
        C5["amount: 40.00, 12.50, 99.90"]
    end

SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY order_date:

  • Row format reads all six columns of every row, including the large notes text.
  • Columnar format reads only order_date and amount. If they are 10% of the bytes, that is roughly 10× less I/O before any other optimisation.

Columnar storage also compresses far better, because a column holds values of one type that are often similar or repeated. Encodings such as dictionary encoding (store PAID/NEW once, then small integers), run-length encoding (store "PAID × 5,000") and delta encoding (for sorted timestamps or IDs) shrink data dramatically before the compression codec even starts.

Row-oriented Column-oriented
Best at Writing and reading whole records Scanning few columns across many rows
Compression Moderate High (similar values together)
Single-row update Cheap Expensive (touches many column chunks)
Typical use OLTP databases, messages, landing raw events Analytics, lakehouse tables
Formats CSV, JSON, Avro Parquet, ORC

2. File formats compared

Format Layout Schema Splittable Compression Schema evolution Best for
CSV Row, text None (header at best) Yes if uncompressed or with a splittable codec Poor, text None; column order matters Exchange with humans and legacy systems
JSON (lines) Row, text, nested Self-describing per record Yes (one object per line) Poor Flexible but untyped APIs, event payloads, landing raw data
Avro Row, binary Embedded schema Yes (sync markers) Good Strong, well-defined rules Kafka messages, write-heavy landing
Parquet Columnar, binary Embedded schema with types Yes (row groups) Excellent Add columns; limited otherwise Analytics, the lakehouse default
ORC Columnar, binary Embedded schema Yes (stripes) Excellent Similar to Parquet Hive ecosystems

Inside a Parquet file

A Parquet file is divided into row groups (often around 128 MB of data), each containing one column chunk per column, each divided into pages. The footer holds the schema and, for each column chunk, statistics such as min, max and null count.

Readers use the footer to:

  • read only the needed column chunks (column pruning), and
  • skip row groups whose min/max cannot match the filter (predicate pushdown), e.g. skip a row group where max(order_date) < '2026-09-01'.

Parquet's weakness is not reading; it is mutation. A Parquet file is immutable. Updating one row means rewriting the whole file. And a folder of Parquet files has no notion of "which files are the current table" — that is the problem table formats solve.

3. Open table formats: what they add over files

A plain folder of Parquet files is not a table. If a job writing 200 files crashes after 120, readers see a half-written table. If two jobs write at once, they can clobber each other. There is no history, no enforced schema, and listing millions of files in object storage is slow.

An open table format adds a metadata layer that records exactly which files make up each version of the table.

---
title: What a table format adds on top of data files
---
flowchart TB
    Q["Query engine<br/>(Spark, Photon, Trino, ...)"] --> M["Table metadata<br/>versions, schema, file list, stats"]
    M --> F1["part-0001.parquet"]
    M --> F2["part-0002.parquet"]
    M --> F3["part-0003.parquet"]
    M -.->|"not referenced by current version"| F4["part-0000.parquet (old)"]
Capability Plain Parquet folder With a table format
Atomic commits No — partial writes are visible Yes — a new version appears all at once or not at all
Concurrent writers Unsafe Optimistic concurrency control with conflict detection
Update / delete / merge Rewrite files manually Built-in DML
Schema enforcement and evolution None Enforced, with controlled evolution
Time travel No Query any retained version
File listing Slow object-store listing Read the file list from metadata
Statistics for skipping Only Parquet footers (must open each file) Per-file stats in metadata, used before opening files

Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg vs Apache Hudi

Delta Lake Apache Iceberg Apache Hudi
Origin Databricks, now Linux Foundation Netflix, now Apache Uber, now Apache
Metadata _delta_log/ of ordered JSON commits plus Parquet checkpoints Tree of metadata file → manifest list → manifests → data files Timeline of actions in .hoodie/
Partitioning Explicit partition columns, or liquid clustering Hidden partitioning with transforms (e.g. days(ts)); partition evolution Explicit partition paths
Update strategy Copy-on-write, with deletion vectors for cheaper deletes/updates Copy-on-write or merge-on-read (delete files) Copy-on-write or merge-on-read
Strength Deep Spark/Databricks integration, simple log model Broad multi-engine support, partition evolution Record-level upserts and incremental pulls
Default on Databricks Many other engines and catalogs (e.g. Snowflake, AWS services, Trino) Some AWS-heavy streaming setups

Convergence is happening: Delta UniForm can write Iceberg-compatible metadata alongside the Delta log so Iceberg readers can read Delta tables, and Unity Catalog can expose tables to Iceberg clients. The practical advice: pick the format your primary engine is best at (Delta on Databricks), and use interoperability features when other engines need to read it.

4. Data warehouse vs data lake vs lakehouse

Data warehouse Data lake Lakehouse
Storage Proprietary, managed by the warehouse Open files in object storage Open files + open table format in object storage
Data types Structured Anything Anything; tables for structured data, volumes for files
Schema On write On read On write for tables, with evolution
Transactions Yes No Yes
Performance Excellent for SQL Varies, often poor without tuning Warehouse-class with good layout and a vectorised engine
ML / data science access Export needed Direct file access Direct access to the same tables
Lock-in High Low Low (open formats)
Classic risk Cost and rigidity Becomes a swamp Needs discipline in layout and governance

The lakehouse idea: store one copy of data in open formats on cheap storage, and point SQL, BI, streaming and ML engines at that copy — instead of maintaining a lake for data science and a warehouse copy for BI.

5. Physical layout: partitioning, bucketing, Z-ordering, liquid clustering

All four techniques try to do one thing: put rows that are queried together into the same files, so filters can skip most files.

5.1 Partitioning

Rows are split into directories by the value of one or more columns:

sales/
  sale_date=2026-09-23/part-0000.parquet
  sale_date=2026-09-24/part-0000.parquet

A query with WHERE sale_date = '2026-09-24' reads one directory (partition pruning).

Rules of thumb:

  • Partition only large tables (roughly 1 TB and up is the common Databricks guidance; below that, partitioning usually hurts more than it helps).
  • Choose a low-cardinality column that is in most filters — typically a date.
  • Aim for each partition to hold at least ~1 GB. Partitioning by customer_id or by timestamp-to-the-second creates millions of tiny files.
  • Never partition by a column you rarely filter on.

5.2 Bucketing

Hash rows into a fixed number of buckets by a column, so two tables bucketed identically can be joined without a shuffle. It is a Hive/Spark table feature; Delta tables do not support bucketing, and on Databricks it has been largely replaced by clustering and AQE.

5.3 Z-ordering

OPTIMIZE t ZORDER BY (customer_id, product_id) rewrites files so that rows close in multi-column space end up in the same files, which tightens each file's min/max range on those columns and improves data skipping. Drawbacks: it is a full rewrite of the targeted data each time, it is not incremental, and its effectiveness drops as you add more columns.

5.4 Liquid clustering

Liquid clustering (Delta Lake) replaces partitioning and Z-ordering for new tables:

CREATE TABLE silver.events (
  event_id STRING, user_id STRING, event_type STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP, payload STRING
) CLUSTER BY (event_type, event_time);

-- Keys can be changed later without rewriting existing data immediately
ALTER TABLE silver.events CLUSTER BY (user_id, event_time);

-- Clustering is applied incrementally by OPTIMIZE
OPTIMIZE silver.events;

Why it is better for most new tables:

  • No partition-size tuning: no tiny partitions from a bad key choice.
  • Incremental: OPTIMIZE only clusters data that is not yet well clustered.
  • Changeable keys: query patterns change; with partitioning, that means a full rewrite.
  • Works for high-cardinality keys where partitioning would explode.
  • On Databricks you can use CLUSTER BY AUTO to let the platform choose keys from query history (where supported).
Technique Granularity Change keys later? Incremental? Use when
Partitioning Directory per value Full rewrite n/a Very large tables with an obvious low-cardinality filter (date), or when you need partition-level operations for retention
Bucketing Fixed hash buckets Full rewrite n/a Non-Delta Hive/Spark tables with repeated joins on the same key
Z-ordering Within files Rewrite No Existing Delta tables not yet on liquid clustering
Liquid clustering Within files, adaptive Yes Yes Default for new Delta tables

6. The small-files problem and compaction

Streaming writes, frequent small batches and over-partitioning all create lots of small files (kilobytes each). Every file costs a metadata entry, an object-store request, a footer read and a task-scheduling slot. A table of 2 million 50 KB files is dramatically slower to read than the same 100 GB in 1,000 files of 100 MB.

---
title: Small files and compaction
---
flowchart LR
    W["Streaming writes<br/>every 30 s"] --> SF["Thousands of<br/>small files"]
    SF --> O["OPTIMIZE<br/>(bin-packing)"]
    O --> LF["Few files of<br/>~100 MB to 1 GB"]
    LF --> R["Fast reads,<br/>better data skipping"]

Fixes, from most to least preferred:

  1. Write fewer, bigger files in the first place. Optimized writes (Delta) shuffle data before writing so each partition gets larger files; avoid over-partitioning; use longer trigger intervals for streams that do not need seconds of latency.
  2. Auto compaction. Delta can run a lightweight compaction after writes when a table has accumulated small files.
  3. Scheduled OPTIMIZE. Bin-packs small files into larger ones (target size is managed automatically on Databricks and tunable via table properties).
  4. Predictive optimization. On Databricks, for Unity Catalog managed tables, the platform can decide when to run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for you.
ALTER TABLE silver.events SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true',
  'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact'   = 'true'
);

-- Liquid-clustered table: OPTIMIZE works out what needs compacting/clustering itself
OPTIMIZE silver.events;

-- Date-partitioned table: limit the rewrite to recent partitions
-- (the WHERE clause may only reference partition columns)
OPTIMIZE silver.page_views WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS;

The opposite problem also exists: files of many GB make parallelism coarse and updates expensive (each MERGE rewrites whole files). Somewhere between ~100 MB and ~1 GB per file is the usual sweet spot, smaller for tables with frequent merges.

7. Compression codecs

Codec Compression ratio Speed Splittable as a whole-file codec Notes
Snappy Moderate Very fast n/a inside Parquet Long-time Parquet default in Spark; good all-rounder
Zstd High Fast (tunable levels) n/a inside Parquet Often 20–40% smaller than snappy at similar read speed; a common modern choice
Gzip High Slow to compress and decompress No Fine for archives; avoid for .csv.gz inputs you need to read in parallel
LZ4 Moderate Very fast n/a inside Parquet Similar trade-off to snappy
Uncompressed None No CPU cost Yes Rarely worth it

Important detail: inside Parquet and ORC, compression is applied per page / column chunk, so the file remains splittable regardless of codec. Splittability only matters for whole-file compression of row formats: one 20 GB events.csv.gz file can only be read by one task, because gzip streams cannot be split.

# Choose the Parquet codec for a Spark session (Delta data files are Parquet)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.compression.codec", "zstd")

8. Putting it together — layout decision guide

Situation Format Layout
Raw JSON events landing from producers Keep original files in a volume or landing path; bronze Delta table with raw payload column Append; liquid clustering on ingestion date if large
Large event fact table (TB+), filtered by date Delta Liquid clustering on (date, frequent filter), or date partitioning if you need partition-level retention
Dimension table (< 1 GB) Delta No partitioning, no clustering needed
Table merged frequently by key Delta with deletion vectors Cluster by the merge key to reduce files touched
Data exchanged with an external partner Parquet (or CSV if they insist) Plain files, documented schema
Kafka messages Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry n/a

Azure / .NET mapping

Concept Azure
Object storage ADLS Gen2 (hierarchical namespace enabled — needed for efficient directory operations)
Paths abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/path
Storage tiers Hot / cool / cold / archive tiers with lifecycle management policies for raw file retention
Lakehouse table format Delta Lake on Azure Databricks; Microsoft Fabric OneLake also stores tables as Delta
Reading Parquet from .NET Parquet.Net library; Apache.Arrow for Arrow data
Querying Delta from other Azure tools Fabric shortcuts, Synapse serverless SQL (Delta reader), Power BI through Databricks SQL

Review checklist

  • I can explain why columnar formats are faster for analytics and how encodings help compression.
  • I know what is inside a Parquet footer and how it enables skipping.
  • I can list what a table format adds over a folder of Parquet files.
  • I can compare Delta, Iceberg and Hudi at a high level.
  • I know the rules of thumb for partitioning and why over-partitioning hurts.
  • I can explain why liquid clustering is preferred over partitioning plus Z-ordering for new Delta tables.
  • I can diagnose and fix a small-files problem.
  • I know why a large .csv.gz file limits parallelism but a zstd Parquet file does not.
